title: Parodos (lines 99–154)

teacherSummary.text: At sunrise the Chorus of Theban elders celebrates the defeat of the Argive army led by Polyneices. They describe Zeus striking down a boastful attacker with lightning and call for dancing and thanks to the gods.

context.history: The Chorus's entrance song (parodos) recalls the war of the Seven against Thebes, a famous myth also staged by Aeschylus.

significance: The city celebrates while the play's real conflict is just beginning. Zeus punishing a "braggart's boast" (line 119) foreshadows the fall of pride later in the play.

items.prompt: Why does the Chorus give only two lines to the brothers in a song about victory?
items.expected: The brothers’ deaths are the one dark note in a song of joy. The Chorus gives them only two lines—“Save two alone, that ill-starred pair … both perished, brother slain by brother” (lines 135–138)—and then calls Victory back and asks that “Memories of war blot out” (lines 139–142). That brevity shows a city eager to forget the war and celebrate, yet it also leaves the question of the brothers open for Creon’s edict.

Sunbeam, of all that ever dawned upon
Our seven-gated Thebes the brightest ray,
O eye of golden day,

anchorPassages.note: The double death that empties the throne and makes Creon's rise possible.
anchorPassages.text:
Seven captains at our seven gates
Thundered; for each a champion waits,
Each left behind his armour bright,
Trophy for Zeus who turns the fight;
Save two alone, that ill-starred pair
One mother to one father bare,
Who lance in rest, one ’gainst the other
Drave, and both perished, brother slain by brother.
Now Victory to Thebes returns again
And smiles upon her chariot-circled plain.
Now let feast and festal shout
Memories of war blot out.
Let us to the temples throng,
Dance and sing the live night long.
God of Thebes, lead thou the round,
Bacchus, shaker of the ground!

weDoAnswers: The Chorus's entrance song (parodos) recalls the war of the Seven against Thebes, a famous myth also staged by Aeschylus. Read closely: “But ere a torch our crown of towers could burn, Ere they had tasted of our blood, they turn Forced by the Dragon; in their rear The din of Ares panic-struck they hear.” (Chorus, lines 115–118).
analysis.weDoWords: “Torch”, “crown of towers” and “panic-struck” stand out in lines 115–118. The city is pictured as crowned with towers that the enemy never got to burn, and Ares is heard as a panic in their rear, so the elders celebrate a rescue that came just in time. The wording turns almost-ruin into thanksgiving.

segments.script: Today's words: braggart — a person who boasts loudly; paean — a song of triumph or thanksgiving; argent — silver in color; pinions — a bird’s wings; impious — showing no respect for the gods; revels — joyful noisy celebrations. “braggart”: Origin: Middle French bragard (“bragging”).

segments.script: The Chorus's entrance song (parodos) recalls the war of the Seven against Thebes, a famous myth also staged by Aeschylus. The city celebrates while the play's real conflict is just beginning. Zeus punishing a "braggart's boast" (line 119) foreshadows the fall of pride later in the play. Imagery: The Parodos fills the night battle with fire, towers and a “forkèd lightning blaze,” so the city’s rescue is felt as something seen and heard, not only told. Structure: The entrance song turns from the war just won to Creon’s summons, so celebration and the new king’s law arrive in one breath. Tone / mood: The elders’ voice is triumphant and grateful, but Zeus’s strike on the “braggart’s boast” already sounds a warning against pride. Watch for burial and the unburied body: The song celebrates a saved city and says nothing yet of Polyneices’s body, so the burial crisis waits just outside the hymn of thanks.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “For Zeus who hates the braggart’s boast / Beheld that gold-bespangled host; / As at the goal the paean they upraise, / He struck them with his forkèd lightning blaze” slowly and put it in my own words: the Chorus says Zeus hates proud boasting, saw the gold-clad Argive army, and struck it with lightning just as the attackers raised a victory hymn. Next, craft. “Braggart’s boast” and “gold-bespangled host” paint the enemy as proud and showy, and the paean is cut off by “forkèd lightning blaze,” so celebration turns into punishment in one breath. The strongest word is “lightning”: it cuts the paean short and turns the victory hymn into a blow. Then, effect. What do lines 119–122 reveal about the city's victory song? My answer: The elders celebrate a rescue that came just in time. Zeus punishing a “braggart’s boast” (line 119) already names the kind of pride the city’s victory song condemns in the defeated host.

segments.script: Ask: What words in this line stand out, and what do they suggest? Expected student answer: “Torch”, “crown of towers” and “panic-struck” stand out. The city is pictured as crowned with towers that the enemy never got to burn, so the elders celebrate a rescue that came just in time. Ask: How does this line connect to divine law and human law? Expected student answer: The elders thank the gods for saving Thebes, so divine power underwrites the city’s victory even before Creon speaks his human edict. (Chorus, lines 115–118.)

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the scene for imagery, structure (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about the city's victory song? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Parodos (lines 99–154) develops the idea of the city's victory song. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and structure shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: The city celebrates while the play's real conflict is just beginning. Zeus punishing a "braggart's boast" (line 119) foreshadows the fall of pride later in the play. When the text says “For Zeus who hates the braggart’s boast / Beheld that gold-bespangled host; / As at the goal the paean they upraise, / He struck them with his forkèd lightning blaze” (Parodos, lines 119–122), it shows this directly. At sunrise the Chorus of Theban elders celebrates the defeat of the Argive army led by Polyneices. They describe Zeus striking down a boastful attacker with lightning and call for dancing and thanks to the gods.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.

items.answerGuidance: Sophocles opens the choral songs with public joy—the rescue of the seven-gated city and thanks to Zeus (lines 115–122, 139–146)—so the private quarrel of the Prologue and the edict that follows stand out more sharply against a city that wants to “blot out” memories of war (lines 141–142).
